Comparison

Ozempic vs Semaglutide

Semaglutide is the active ingredient and Ozempic is one finished product made with it: Novo Nordisk's type 2 diabetes medicine, a weekly injection and, since a January 2026 FDA approval, also a daily tablet.14

Key differences

A product versus an ingredient

Semaglutide is what is inside the pen; Ozempic is the pen, the formulation and the label. Three US brands contain semaglutide: Ozempic, Rybelsus and Wegovy.135 Ozempic's label is limited to adults with type 2 diabetes. It covers blood sugar control, lowering major cardiovascular event risk in those with established cardiovascular disease (added January 16, 2020), and lowering kidney decline, kidney failure and cardiovascular death risk in those with chronic kidney disease (added January 28, 2025).12 Weight loss is not one of its approved uses.1 FDA also approved the 2 mg weekly dose on March 28, 2022.2

What Ozempic adds to semaglutide

The ingredient has a fixed chemistry. The label gives the formula C187H291N45O59 and a molecular weight of 4113.58 g/mol.1 PubChem files it as CID 56843331, and its CAS registry number is 910463-68-2.1211 Semaglutide shares 94% of its sequence with human GLP-1, its peptide backbone is made by yeast fermentation, and its half-life is about 1 week, mainly because it binds to albumin in the blood.1 Steady blood levels take 4 to 5 weeks of weekly doses, and the drug stays in the blood for about 5 weeks after the last one.1

The product adds everything around that molecule. Each mL of the pen solution also holds disodium phosphate dihydrate (1.42 mg), propylene glycol (14 mg) and phenol (5.5 mg) in water for injection, at a pH of about 7.4. The single-dose syringes use sodium chloride in place of the propylene glycol and phenol.1 Ozempic arrives as a ready-made clear liquid with no mixing step, and its instructions say never to draw it out of the pen with a syringe.1 The pens come in three sizes: the 2 mg per 3 mL pen gives 0.25 mg or 0.5 mg doses, the 4 mg pen gives 1 mg doses and the 8 mg pen gives 2 mg doses.1

One brand name, two routes

Since January 30, 2026, the Ozempic name has covered a tablet too. FDA approved a supplement that renamed Rybelsus formulation R2 as Ozempic tablets, and the tablets sit on the Rybelsus application, NDA 213051.413 Ozempic tablets come in 1.5, 4 and 9 mg, and Rybelsus in 3, 7 and 14 mg; the label says the two tablet brands are not interchangeable milligram for milligram.3 The tablet schedule starts at 1.5 mg a day for 30 days, a starter dose that does not control blood sugar, then 4 mg, with 4 or 9 mg from day 61.3 The label allows people on the 0.5 mg weekly injection to switch to tablets one week after their last shot, on the prescriber's decision.3

Semaglutide that is not Ozempic

Several kinds of product use the word semaglutide without being Ozempic. Counterfeit pens are one. FDA has found counterfeit Ozempic 1 mg in the US drug supply chain three times: it had seized thousands of units by December 2023, seized several hundred units from lot PAR0362 on April 9, 2025, and seized dozens more from lot PAR1229 in late 2025.6 FDA advises patients to get Ozempic only with a valid prescription through state-licensed pharmacies and to check the product for signs of counterfeiting before use.6

Compounded and research-labeled products are others. Compounded semaglutide is not FDA approved, and FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed.7 FDA has also warned companies that illegally sold unapproved semaglutide falsely labeled "for research purposes" or "not for human consumption" directly to consumers for human use, with dosing instructions. It calls these products of unknown quality and urges consumers not to purchase them.7 The label facts on this page describe Ozempic as Novo Nordisk makes it, not any other semaglutide product.

Outside the United States

The brand map differs abroad. The European Commission authorized Ozempic across the EU on February 8, 2018, for adults whose type 2 diabetes is not satisfactorily controlled, either alone when metformin cannot be used or added to other diabetes medicines.9 On March 26, 2026, the EU gave a conditional authorization to Kayshild, a semaglutide injection for adults with non-cirrhotic MASH and moderate to advanced fibrosis.10 In the US, that liver use sits on the Wegovy label instead.5

Frequently asked questions

Is Ozempic the same as semaglutide?

Not exactly. Semaglutide is the drug substance, a GLP-1 analog and receptor agonist. Ozempic is a finished Novo Nordisk medicine built around it, with its own formulation, pens, doses and label for adults with type 2 diabetes.1 The same substance is in Rybelsus tablets, at different doses, and in Wegovy, which has different doses and approved uses.35 So every Ozempic dose is semaglutide, but semaglutide is not always Ozempic.

Is Ozempic approved for weight loss?

No. The Ozempic label covers three uses in adults with type 2 diabetes: blood sugar control, lowering major cardiovascular event risk in those with established cardiovascular disease, and lowering kidney and cardiovascular risks in those with chronic kidney disease.1 People did lose weight in its diabetes trials, about 5.6 kg on 1 mg and 6.4 kg on 2 mg over 40 weeks.1 The semaglutide brand approved for weight reduction is Wegovy.5

Can Ozempic be taken orally?

Yes, since January 30, 2026. On that date FDA approved renaming a once-daily semaglutide tablet, Rybelsus formulation R2, to Ozempic tablets.4 They come in 1.5, 4 and 9 mg. The label says to take one each morning on an empty stomach with up to 4 ounces of plain water and wait at least 30 minutes before eating or drinking.3 The weekly Ozempic pen is a separate product with its own dosing.

Is Ozempic a peptide?

Yes. Its active ingredient, semaglutide, is a modified peptide: a GLP-1 analog with 94% sequence homology to human GLP-1. Its peptide backbone is made by yeast fermentation, and it carries a fatty diacid chain; binding to albumin in the blood gives it a half-life of about one week.1 Ozempic itself is a prescription medicine: FDA's application record lists its products with prescription status, apart from one older pen size marked discontinued.2

Is compounded semaglutide the same as Ozempic?

No. Compounded semaglutide is not FDA approved, and FDA does not review compounded drugs for safety, effectiveness or quality before they are marketed.7 FDA has received adverse event reports, some requiring hospitalization, that may be related to dosing errors with compounded semaglutide in multiple-dose vials. The errors came from patients measuring wrong doses and from providers miscalculating doses, and confusion between milliliters, milligrams and 'units' may have contributed.8
